w: What's tested Occlusal trauma: the definition, and primary vs secondary (normal vs reduced support); the difference is clinical, not histologic Unilateral vs jiggling forces, and the hourglass The signs: clinical (fremitus and the rest) and radiographic (a widened PDL and the rest); a vertical defect doesn't mean occlusal trauma Mobility: what it depends on, what causes it, how it's graded, and why it's a sign of adaptation What the animal experiments showed: trauma alone, trauma with gingivitis, trauma with periodontitis Occlusal discrepancies and occlusal adjustment: what it does and doesn't do, and when to do it His conclusions, the bottom line This lecture is Dr. Abou-Arraj's (periodontics), the one hour of occlusion at the start of the 11/12 session, before the Perio course took over. Dr. Givan asked him to cover how occlusion affects the periodontium, "or does it affect it?" Most of the literature is classic: there has been no new information in this field for many years. He walked through it to show why we are where we are today, then gave the bottom line. When a student asked, he said not to go into the weeds: "You don't need to learn all the names and such. Conclusions are enough." The researchers' names below are only there to follow the story. Occlusal trauma: the definition Occlusal trauma is "injury resulting in tissue changes within the periodontal attachment apparatus as a result of occlusal force(s)" (the 1999 International Workshop's consensus). The occlusal force is the initiating factor; the injury that results in the periodontium is what we call occlusal trauma. It is the term we use when we suspect that occlusion is contributing to periodontal disease. The injury itself is histologic, seen as bone loss, a widened PDL space, mobility, or teeth moving out of position. Primary vs secondary occlusal trauma There are two kinds: The forces Traumatic (excessive) occlusal forces Normal or traumatic occlusal forces The support Normal: normal bone level, normal attachment level Reduced: bone loss and attachment loss already present In short The tooth hasn't lost a single millimeter of attachment or bone Even a normal force can injure a tooth that has lost support Why can a normal force injure a tooth with reduced support? With normal support, the tooth's center of rotation is generally in the mid-root; with reduced support it moves apically, toward the apical third. His analogy is the fence post: with two thirds of it in the ground, lean on it and it probably won't move; with only a third, or 20%, in the ground, the same lean (same force, same mass, same everything) may tip it over. The distinction between primary and secondary is clinical, exactly as described. Histologically, the changes trauma from occlusion causes in the periodontium are the same in both. So "primary occlusal trauma on #8" should tell you #8 has zero attachment loss and zero bone loss. The slides add that symptoms develop only when the load is so high that the periodontium can't withstand and distribute it with the tooth's position and stability unchanged. Unilateral and jiggling forces A unilateral force acts in one direction: pressure on one side and tension on the other. Orthodontics uses it: tipping (the crown leans, mesially or distally, to position the tooth in the arch) or bodily movement (the whole tooth, root and crown, moves in one direction). Orthodontics does controlled, unilateral movement, not jiggling. A jiggling force comes from one side and then from the other: once from the mesial and once from the distal, or once from the facial and once from the lingual. Because the tooth is pushed both ways, there is pressure and tension on both sides, and the net result is an hourglass shape around the tooth: a widened PDL, bone loss on both sides, and mobility. The slides call this "often the clinical situation in humans." Two more terms from the perio course: a healthy reduced periodontium is a stable periodontium after periodontal treatment, with bone and attachment loss but no inflammation or deepened probing depths. Horizontal bone loss runs parallel to the line connecting the CEJs of neighboring teeth; vertical (angular) bone loss is oblique to it, the V-shaped defect. Signs and symptoms Occlusal trauma can only be confirmed histologically, and we don't do histology on patients. The clinical and radiographic findings are surrogate indicators of it. In the slides' words, "occlusal trauma" is a diagnosis, not a finding. Clinical indicators: Progressive mobility: Class 1 today, Class 2 when you see the patient three months later. Tooth migration: the tooth is no longer where it was (pathologic tooth migration). Fremitus: a palpable or visible movement of a tooth when subjected to occlusal forces, sometimes called functional mobility. To test it, have the patient tap their teeth together while you rest a finger on the facial gingiva: if you feel the tooth move under your finger, it is being pushed every time the teeth meet. When it's advanced you can see it without a finger. It shows mostly on anterior teeth. Fremitus isn't part of the mobility classification, but a tooth with fremitus usually has Class 3 mobility. Occlusal prematurities or discrepancies: a non-working contact, or a slide from CR to CO of more than 1 mm. Wear facets, from grinding. Fractured teeth: a cusp or an incisal edge, from a force too heavy for it. Thermal sensitivity or pain on biting. His patient example shows several at once: spaces that weren't there before, opening as the teeth lost support (the upper teeth can only move facially and a little down), a fractured incisal tip that turned out to come from the occlusion, not a blow, and wear facets on several teeth. Radiographic indicators: A widened PDL space. In health the space is roughly 0.25 mm; a wider radiolucent band around the tooth suggests the tooth is likely mobile (confirm it clinically), under forces that shift it in more than one direction. A discontinued or thickened lamina dura: it can go either way (thicker and more radiopaque, or a line that disappears and reappears as you trace it around the tooth). Bone loss: in a furcation, vertical, or circumferential. Root resorption, in some cases. He wanted one thing very clear: just because you see a vertical defect, do not assume there is occlusal trauma. It isn't cause and effect. The opposite may be more true: if there is occlusal trauma and bone loss, the bone loss is likely to be more vertical. And any of these clinical or radiographic signs can exist without occlusal trauma. Tooth mobility and occlusal trauma A tooth's horizontal mobility depends on the height of the alveolar bone, the width of the PDL, and the shape and number of roots (a single-rooted tooth moves more easily than a multi-rooted one). When a tooth becomes mobile, the possible causes are: Progression of periodontal disease: lost attachment and bone. Overloading, or occlusal trauma: a Class II, an MOD or a crown left high, so the tooth is the first contact every time the patient closes. It may become uncomfortable or painful on biting, and it will become mobile. A periapical lesion: an infection or abscess at the apex. Periodontal surgery: after a flap on a quadrant (resective surgery), expect the teeth to be slightly mobile for up to a year; they settle down. Measuring it: move the tooth buccolingually between two rigid instruments. The scale on his slide (Miller's): 0 Physiologic mobility, 0.1-0.2 mm horizontally: no movement you can see 1 Increased mobility of the crown, at most 1 mm horizontally 2 Visibly increased mobility, more than 1 mm horizontally 3 Severe: horizontal and vertical (press on the occlusal surface and it moves up into the socket), impinging on function Careful: Dr. Givan's L7 handout grades Miller's index differently (1 = barely distinguishable, 2 = any horizontal movement up to 1 mm, 3 = more than 1 mm, or depressed or rotated). Both put vertical (depressible) movement in the top grade. When a question names this lecture, use Dr. Abou-Arraj's scale. Mobility is a sign of adaptation of the periodontal tissues to the forces on the tooth, excessive or normal, on a healthy or a reduced periodontium. Mobility is not a bad thing in itself: a tooth with Class 2 mobility doesn't have a hopeless prognosis, and you shouldn't jump to extracting and replacing it. Class 3 is tougher and makes the prognosis much worse. Either way, look for why the tooth is mobile and what you can do about it. Mobile teeth respond less well to treatment, whether regenerative treatment or soft tissue grafting. Class 1 doesn't affect it as much as Class 2, so for a Class 2 tooth, adjust the occlusion to bring it to Class 1 or less, if you can. In the slides' words (Lindhe and Ericsson): permanent increased mobility has no influence on the development of periodontal disease, but healing after periodontal treatment may be better in non-mobile than in mobile teeth. Does occlusion cause periodontal disease? The history About 100 years ago, people thought heavy occlusion caused periodontitis ("pyorrhea alveolaris"), and the treatment they suggested was to flatten the cusps of every patient with signs of occlusal trauma; occlusal therapy was considered mandatory. They even thought Stillman's clefts and McCall's festoons on the gingival margin came from occlusal forces cutting off the gingiva's blood supply. Perfusion studies refuted that: the gingiva's blood supply is external to the alveolus. It has three sources: the PDL arteries, the intra-alveolar arteries through the bone, and the supraperiosteal arteries, the main supply to the marginal gingiva. Animal studies in the 1930s suggested occlusion is at least a contributing factor. Then one of the first human autopsy studies described periodontal disease the way we understand it today, an inflammatory process starting at the gingival attachment and spreading into the bone along the blood vessels, and found no evidence that occlusion caused or influenced it. The cadaver studies: co-destruction or plaque alone? Two groups studied human cadavers: the histopathology of the lesions, how far plaque reached apically, the teeth's mobility, and their occlusion. A cadaver is a single snapshot in time, so these studies have limited value for cause and effect. Their conclusions conflicted: Co-destruction (Glickman): plaque inflammation alone stays in the zone of irritation (the marginal and interdental gingiva) and causes gingivitis, and its spread leads to horizontal bone loss. Traumatic occlusion acts on the zone of co-destruction (the PDL, the alveolar bone and the cementum; in class he included the transseptal fibers, which the slides draw as the boundary between the zones) and changes the pathway of the inflammation into it, giving vertical defects. Occlusion is a co-destructive factor added to the bacterial insult. Plaque alone (Waerhaug): couldn't find that. Attachment and bone loss came from the inflammation of subgingival plaque alone, and a tooth with more bone loss than its neighbor had plaque further apically: "track the plaque." Vertical defects formed whether or not there was occlusal trauma. That left no answer to what to do about signs of occlusal trauma: adjust everybody, or just treat the plaque? The animal experiments of the 1970s Two groups did large series of studies: one in Rochester, New York, with squirrel monkeys, and one in Gothenburg, Sweden, with beagle dogs. The disease Silk ligatures and no hygiene: plaque-induced, mild to moderate (suprabony pockets) Flaps raised and bony defects made surgically, plus plaque: advanced (infrabony pockets) The trauma A wooden wedge between two teeth, moved to the other side every 48 hours: a moderate force, like an orthodontic force A cap splint in hyperocclusion with a spring bar on a premolar: pushed out every time the dog closed, pulled back when it opened, a severe, true jiggling force (In class he called the wedges a jiggling force too; the slides' summary calls them non-jiggling, next to the dogs' true jiggling.) What they found: Occlusal trauma alone (both groups) Increased mobility; loss of bone density (more radiolucent, but no loss of crestal bone height); no loss of attachment; a return to pretreatment stability once the trauma was removed Trauma plus inflammation on a normal periodontium (gingivitis) Increased mobility; greater loss of bone density; still no attachment loss Trauma plus inflammation on a reduced periodontium (periodontitis) The groups disagreed. Beagle dogs: attachment and bone loss beyond what the disease caused alone ("co-destruction is a reality"). Squirrel monkeys: no further attachment loss beyond the disease alone ("co-destruction is a question") So trauma alone is not a primary factor: do this damage, and things get bad, but stop it in time and they become stable again. With gingivitis there is still no irreversible damage. Where a tooth with periodontitis can't withstand jiggling forces, the PDL space, the mobility, the bone loss (in height) and the clinical attachment loss all increase. In the monkeys, 10 weeks after the trauma stopped, the bone regained its density. But 10 weeks after stopping the trauma without treating the periodontitis, there was no return to stability: stopping the occlusal trauma does not reverse periodontitis. You still have to treat the periodontitis. The animal conclusions: without inflammation, occlusal trauma doesn't cause irreversible bone loss or loss of attachment; taken together, occlusal trauma is not a causative agent (a primary etiologic factor) of periodontal disease. But animal models and the short duration of the studies leave questions about what it means for humans, and we can't do these studies in humans. ("I would argue we shouldn't be doing them in animals either.") Human studies: occlusal discrepancies The first human studies only reviewed charts, study models and radiographs, with no direct patient examinations. One found that non-working contacts may initiate trauma from occlusion, TMJ problems or bruxism, and that molars with non-working contacts had more bone loss, more mobility and deeper probing depths. Another, about 20 years later, found no association. In the occlusal trauma and periodontal literature, an occlusal discrepancy is one or both of: a slide from CR to CO of more than 1 mm, and non-working contacts in lateral movements. Why, and when, do they have to be treated? The randomized trial (often cited to justify what we do): 50 patients with periodontitis, randomly assigned to occlusal adjustment or none, and all of them got all the periodontal treatment they needed, non-surgical or surgical. After two years, the adjusted group had a better gain in clinical attachment (about 0.5 mm) but no difference in probing depth. Attachment gain held over time says something about long-term healing, where a drop in probing depth can come from the tissue shrinking after a good SRP. Initial mobility, Class 1 or Class 2, didn't affect the result. Two camps remain. For adjustment: that trial, and a study in which teeth with occlusal discrepancies had deeper initial probing depths, more mobility and poorer prognoses than teeth without. Careful patient selection: not every occlusal discrepancy causes occlusal trauma, so not every discrepancy in a patient with periodontitis needs to be adjusted. That camp doesn't say never adjust; it says choose who gets adjusted. When to adjust Except in acute conditions, occlusion is addressed during initial therapy, after efforts to reduce or minimize the inflammatory lesion. An acute condition is, for example, fremitus or a heavily loaded tooth at the first exam: then he might adjust the occlusion early. Otherwise, start with the usual periodontal treatment (oral hygiene instructions, scaling and root planing, the rest of phase 1), keep monitoring the teeth you suspect have occlusal trauma throughout therapy, and at the phase 1 re-evaluation, adjust the occlusion if they haven't improved with periodontal treatment alone. His conclusions Occlusal trauma does not cause gingivitis or periodontitis. It does affect the supporting periodontal tissues: "absolutely yes." There is a lack of evidence from human studies implicating occlusal trauma in the progression of attachment loss in periodontitis (the only evidence came from one group's animal studies). Occlusal trauma produces bone resorption in density, and necrosis of the PDL, even without inflammation: a radiograph may show more radiolucent bone, a widened PDL or a discontinued lamina dura, but no loss of bone height from occlusal trauma alone. These changes are reversible once the offending forces are eliminated, and the tissues don't repair until they are. Occlusal adjustment may reduce the mobility of traumatized teeth and promote the regrowth of bone, but it will not arrest the breakdown caused by plaque. You still have to control the plaque. Healing after periodontal therapy may be better in non-mobile than in mobile teeth. When it's done, adjusting occlusal discrepancies should follow successful anti-infective periodontal therapy. Like antibiotics (Dr. Litz's lecture), it's not where you start: treat the inflammation first, then adjust the occlusion if there's still room for it. This fits Dr. Givan's L7: occlusal trauma usually shows up in the attachment apparatus, and whether bone loss is reversible depends on the connective tissue attachment, which inflammation affects and occlusion doesn't.
